newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. JULY RETAIL SALES UP 0.6 PCT.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. JULY RETAIL SALES UP 0.6 PCT.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department said retail sales rose 0.6 percent in July compared to a revised 0.7 percent jump in the previous month. The number excluding automobiles was up 0.5 percent.
Economists in a Reuters survey had expected a 0.7 percent rise in overall retail sales and a 0.5 percent excluding cars.
THOMAS CARPENTER, ECONOMIST, ABS CAPITAL MANAGEMENT: "This is a reinforcing statistic. It's about what was expected."

"Given the fact that the full effect of the jump in auto sales ... in July from June was not fully reflected in this number, what we have to worry about next month, at least bond people will start to worry about, is what will the revision be for these numbers."

JAMES PADINHA, ECONOMIST, BRIEFING.COM: "They probably weren't as bad as people were expecting, but we think they are real solid ... We are looking specifically at June which was up a couple tenths on both counts, and ex-auto July gain."

"What we see is a couple more of these 0.5 percent gains -- July, August, September -- translates roughly into a 3.3 percent Q3 consumption rate. We were up in the four percents in Q1, people got overenthused about that dip in Q2 and now it looks like the consumer is coming back almost as strong as he was in the first quarter."

RAM BHAGAVATULA, CHIEF FINANCIAL ECONOMIST, CITICORP GLOBAL FINANCE: "Retail sales came in as expected. The market has to figure out where we are going next. People were quite concerned about an explosion in retail sales.

"With June, on a back-to-back basis, sales were reasonably good -- up 0.7 percent and up 0.5 percent, respectively. So the focus will have to shift to August to see what will happen to August sales. I can't imagine the UPS strike will affect a very big piece of total sales."
ASTRID ADOLFSON, SENIOR VICE PRESIDENT, MCM MONEYWATCH: "When you look at the (overall retail sales number), it's rising at a moderate rate, which confirms that the consumer is back spending.
"(But they are) not spending at a five or six percent rate, but more likely at a two to three percent (rate) that the Fed is comfortable with."
